packet.description_seed: Alberta's decision to hold a referendum on separation has been widely criticised, including the separatists who say the question is not definitive enough.

what: Carney says Alberta is 'essential' to Canada as province plans vote on separation

clean_source_blocks.text: Alberta's decision to hold a referendum on separation has been widely criticised, including the separatists who say the question is not definitive enough.

Alberta premier calls for referendum on secession after judge ruled initiative to force binding vote invalid The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, has said that Alberta is “essential” to the country’s future, hours after the province’s leader moved the oil-rich region closer toward a referendum on independence. Separatists in the western province spent months collecting signatures seeking to trigger a binding October vote on seceding from the nation. On 4 May, they delivered their petition to provincial officials, insisting they had collected more than enough names to force a vote under Alberta law. But an Alberta judge shut down the process, saying the citizens’ initiative was invalid because the separatists had failed to consult with Indigenous groups whose rights could be threatened if the province separated from Canada.

A day after Alberta announced it will hold a referendum on whether it should remain in Canada or hold a binding vote on separation, Prime Minister Mark Carney called the western province an "essential" part of the country. Speaking on Friday, Carney praised the "huge contributions" the province has made and said his government is working to improve Canada, Alberta included. "We're renovating the country as we go, and Alberta being at the centre of that is essential," Carney said as he toured work being done on Canada's parliament building. The vote on Alberta's future is the first significant test of the country's unity in decades. There has been a growing separatist movement in recent years in the oil-rich province, fuelled in part by a belief that it is overlooked by decision-makers in Ottawa.

In an address late on Thursday, Alberta’s premier, Danielle Smith, called the judge’s decision “erroneous”, charging that it “interferes with the democratic rights of hundreds of thousands of Albertans”. Smith, a conservative whose political coalition includes separatists, said she supported “Alberta remaining in Canada”. But she insisted she would not let “a legal mistake by a single judge” quash a debate that needed to take place. “It’s time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject and move on,” she said. In October, she plans to ask Albertans if they want her government “to commence the legal process necessary to hold a binding referendum” on independence. Smith said she had structured her question such that it does not violate the judge’s ruling, because it “does not directly trigger separation”.

payload.title: Carney korostaa Albertan merkitystä Kanadalle provinssin valmistellessa äänestystä
payload.summary: Kanadan pääministeri Mark Carney sanoo Albertan olevan olennainen osa maan tulevaisuutta, kun provinssi valmistelee äänestystä, joka voi avata tien sitovaan kansanäänestykseen itsenäisyydestä.
payload.content:
Kanadan pääministeri Mark Carney on korostanut Albertan merkitystä Kanadalle sen jälkeen, kun provinssi ilmoitti aikovansa järjestää äänestyksen siitä, pitäisikö sen pysyä Kanadassa vai edetä kohti sitovaa äänestystä irtautumisesta. Länsi-Kanadassa sijaitsevassa öljyrikkaassa provinssissa separatistinen liike on vahvistunut viime vuosina, ja kysymys on noussut yhdeksi maan yhtenäisyyden merkittävimmistä koetuksista vuosikymmeniin.

## Carney painotti Albertan panosta

Carney sanoi perjantaina, että Alberta on Kanadan tulevaisuudelle välttämätön. Hän kiitti provinssin suurta panosta maalle ja sanoi hallituksensa pyrkivän parantamaan Kanadaa myös Albertan näkökulmasta.

Pääministerin mukaan Alberta on keskeisessä asemassa, kun maata uudistetaan. Kommentit annettiin sen jälkeen, kun provinssin johto oli vienyt eteenpäin suunnitelmaa äänestyksestä, joka liittyy mahdolliseen itsenäisyysprosessiin.

Albertan separatismia on ruokkinut muun muassa kokemus siitä, että provinssin näkemykset jäävät Ottawan päätöksenteossa liian vähälle huomiolle. Provinssin taloudellinen merkitys perustuu vahvasti energiasektoriin, mikä on tehnyt sen suhteesta liittovaltion politiikkaan ajoittain jännitteisen.

## Smith haluaa äänestyksen oikeuden päätöksestä huolimatta

Albertan pääministeri Danielle Smith ilmoitti torstai-iltana tukevansa äänestystä, vaikka oikeus oli aiemmin katsonut kansalaisaloitteen sitovasta eroa koskevasta kansanäänestyksestä pätemättömäksi. Tuomarin mukaan aloitteen valmistelussa ei ollut kuultu alkuperäiskansoja, joiden oikeuksiin Albertan mahdollinen irtautuminen Kanadasta voisi vaikuttaa.

Separatistit olivat keränneet allekirjoituksia pyrkien käynnistämään lokakuussa sitovan äänestyksen provinssin eroamisesta. He toimittivat vetoomuksensa provinssin viranomaisille 4. toukokuuta ja sanoivat keränneensä riittävästi nimiä Albertan lain mukaisen äänestyksen järjestämiseksi.

Smith kutsui oikeuden ratkaisua virheelliseksi ja sanoi sen puuttuvan satojentuhansien albertalaisten demokraattisiin oikeuksiin. Hän on kuitenkin myös sanonut kannattavansa Albertan pysymistä Kanadassa. Smithin mukaan tarkoituksena on selvittää albertalaisten tahto ja jatkaa sen jälkeen eteenpäin.

Lokakuuksi suunnitellussa äänestyksessä albertalaisilta kysyttäisiin, haluavatko he provinssihallituksen aloittavan oikeudellisen prosessin, joka tarvitaan sitovan itsenäisyysäänestyksen järjestämiseksi. Smithin mukaan kysymys on muotoiltu niin, ettei se suoraan käynnistä eroa Kanadasta eikä siten riko oikeuden ratkaisua.
summary_bullets: Mark Carney sanoo Albertan olevan olennainen osa Kanadan tulevaisuutta.
Alberta valmistelee lokakuuksi äänestystä mahdollisen sitovan itsenäisyysäänestyksen käynnistämisestä.
Oikeus oli aiemmin katsonut separatistien kansalaisaloitteen pätemättömäksi alkuperäiskansojen kuulemisen puutteiden vuoksi.

Alberta's decision to hold a referendum on separation has been widely criticised, including the separatists who say the question is not definitive enough.

Alberta premier calls for referendum on secession after judge ruled initiative to force binding vote invalid The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, has said that Alberta is “essential” to the country’s future, hours after the province’s leader moved the oil-rich region closer toward a referendum on independence. Separatists in the western province spent months collecting signatures seeking to trigger a binding October vote on seceding from the nation. On 4 May, they delivered their petition to provincial officials, insisting they had collected more than enough names to force a vote under Alberta law. But an Alberta judge shut down the process, saying the citizens’ initiative was invalid because the separatists had failed to consult with Indigenous groups whose rights could be threatened if the province separated from Canada.

A day after Alberta announced it will hold a referendum on whether it should remain in Canada or hold a binding vote on separation, Prime Minister Mark Carney called the western province an "essential" part of the country. Speaking on Friday, Carney praised the "huge contributions" the province has made and said his government is working to improve Canada, Alberta included. "We're renovating the country as we go, and Alberta being at the centre of that is essential," Carney said as he toured work being done on Canada's parliament building. The vote on Alberta's future is the first significant test of the country's unity in decades. There has been a growing separatist movement in recent years in the oil-rich province, fuelled in part by a belief that it is overlooked by decision-makers in Ottawa.

In an address late on Thursday, Alberta’s premier, Danielle Smith, called the judge’s decision “erroneous”, charging that it “interferes with the democratic rights of hundreds of thousands of Albertans”. Smith, a conservative whose political coalition includes separatists, said she supported “Alberta remaining in Canada”. But she insisted she would not let “a legal mistake by a single judge” quash a debate that needed to take place. “It’s time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject and move on,” she said. In October, she plans to ask Albertans if they want her government “to commence the legal process necessary to hold a binding referendum” on independence. Smith said she had structured her question such that it does not violate the judge’s ruling, because it “does not directly trigger separation”.
